content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a kind of efficient CNN component, including pointwise and depthwise convolutions,  conducted the experiments for the proposed models' performance, and further demonstrated the proposed models' hardware efficacy on FPGA. Additionally, the authors also proposed a kind of channel pruning scheme for shift layers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This paper conducted experiments on FPGA and evaluated the speed-up property of the proposed methods.

Weaknesses:
- This paper's novelty cannot meet the bar of the ICLR. (1) The idea of shift layer pruning is ok, however, it is mostly a technological advancement. (2) The past study conducted CP convolution[1] by decomposing the 4-D kernel tensor and performing the CONV layer into two DW and PW operations. This paper also uses CP decomposition. The difference is that this paper unfolded the 4-D kernel into a 3-D shape by merging the two kernel window modes, which is a common operation without much novelty. Furthermore, the proposed CP convolution, introduced as the pointwise-depthwise-pointwise arrangement in this paper, is a specific example of Tucker convolution[2] as shown in Figure 3 of [2].

- The experiment results are not well presented. Only CIFAR and TinyImageNet are used, and the performance is unsatisfactory. Moreover, many existing tensorized CNN (e.g., TT-CNN, TR-CNN[3]) are not compared in the experiments part.

- The layout of this paper needs to be re-optimized. For example, Figure 1 is blurry, and 300 dpi is recommended. 


[1] Vadim, Lebedev, et al. "Speeding-up convolutional neural networks using fine-tuned cp-decomposition." arXiv preprint arXiv:1412.6553 (2014).

[2] Jean, Kossaifi, et al. "Factorized higher-order cnns with an application to spatio-temporal emotion estimation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2020.

[3] Yu, Pan, Maolin Wang, and Zenglin Xu. "TedNet: A Pytorch toolkit for tensor decomposition networks." Neurocomputing 469 (2022): 234-238.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Medium.

content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed a kind of efficient CNN component. However, the layout is not clear enough. And more importantly, the novelty is limited and cannot reach the bar of ICLR, so I tend to reject it.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies decomposition of the convolutional layers in CNNs. 

The paper tries to visually explain (give intuition) about different ways to approximate convolutions. Mainly, depending on the "slices" along which the kenrels are considered - different approximations will include blocks similar to the ones of popular mobile networks (mobile net, etc...).

The paper then presents a set of experiments on a very easy, and well studied datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
It is not clear what are the novel contributions of this work.

The way to visualize and list different approximations based on how the kernel tensor is sliced is cute - but far from a novelty worth a paper at this venue.

The authors also use extremely easy and well studied dataasets for experiments, which is not enough to make strong conclusions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is hard to follow. The abstract introduces undefined term in the first sentence; the rest of the abstract is very hard to follow and seems like a kitchen sink of catchwords.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors claim a discovery of the unifying tensor view - "a neat started to CNN approximation theory". I disagree. These concepts are very well known in the area. Several papers have addressed convolution decomposition with much more precise mathematical definition and analysis of approximation errors.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied the weight compression task of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) via tensor decomposition. In particular, the 4D kernels are first reshaped into  3D tensors by merging the modes associated with the spatial space and then represented in the CP format. The authors claim that such a framework (with several additional tricks, e.g., the one-hot kernel filters) can be used to universally model a wide range of CNN architectures. The proposed framework also gives better geometric and arithmetic intuition compared to the existing works such as (Hayashi, 2019)
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength:

1. The paper focused on a practically important problem, which helps realize the implementation of large-scale neural nets on resource-limited devices. It is so exciting that the experimental results on FPGA are illustrated in the paper.
2. Some related new architectures like the ShiftNet are taken into the tensor framework, which seems to be the first time.

### Weakness

1. Section 4, as the main body of the paper, is *very* hard to follow. I am still very confused with how the introduced technical details support the central claim of the paper, even though I have gone through this part more than three times. The attached illustrative figures are too complicated and unclear, so they are totally useless for readers to understand the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. As aforementioned, the manuscript's clarity should be carefully improved. For example, at the beginning, the paper highlights the unique advantage of the proposed method on the better geometric and arithmetic intuition compared with the existing works. However, apart from the trick of merging the modes associated with the spatial space, I cannot find anything essentially different from (Hayashi et al., 2019). Furthermore, there is also no clear discussion on how the better intuition helps us in practice. 

2. Please simplify Fig. 1 and 3. There is rich information contained in Fig. 1 for example, but it lacks the *clear* introduction to the meanings of each symbol. Sometimes, more straightforward graphs might be better for readers to catch your main ideas easily.

3. More practical datasets should be used for the performance evaluation in the experiments. This paper focuses on the model compression problem, which is more close to real-world applications, it is thus so important to show solid experimental results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Although many experimental results are shown in the paper, only tiny datasets are exploited. We all know that in deep learning the superior performance on tiny nets and datasets does NOT mean the advantages on larger ones. The lack of evaluation of the proposed methods on larger datasets makes me suspect that performance improvement is still in practice.
content.summary_of_the_review: My score is mainly based on the clarity issue of the manuscript. I think this would be a good paper (I can raise the score) if the clarity can be improved, even though the experimental results remain in the current situation.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
